name: Is CBD legal? Federal CBD rules
where_it_stands: CBD from hemp is legal to grow and sell as a hemp product, but the FDA says it cannot be added to food or sold as a dietary supplement, and from 11 December 2026 full-spectrum products with more than 0.4 mg of total THC per container lose federal hemp status. Since April 2026 a Medicare pilot has let some providers give patients up to $500 a year of hemp-derived products, and the FDA said it would not act against qualifying oral CBD used that way.

next_milestone.text: The 0.4 mg per-container cap on total THC and similar cannabinoids takes effect for finished hemp products, including many full-spectrum CBD products.

summary: CBD (cannabidiol) is a non-intoxicating cannabinoid. The 2018 Farm Bill made hemp-derived CBD legal to produce, but the FDA has approved only one CBD drug, Epidiolex, for certain seizure disorders, and it says CBD is excluded from the dietary supplement definition and may not be added to food sold across state lines. In January 2023 the agency said existing food and supplement rules were not suited to CBD, denied petitions to allow it in supplements and asked Congress for a new framework; Congress has not created one. The November 2025 hemp law keeps CBD itself within the hemp definition but caps finished products at 0.4 mg of total THC and similar cannabinoids per container, which catches many full-spectrum oils and gummies once it applies on 11 December 2026. President Trump asked Congress in April 2026 to change the law so full-spectrum CBD stays available. Separately, CMS's Substance Access Beneficiary Engagement Incentive, which began on 1 April 2026, lets participants in certain Medicare models give eligible patients up to $500 a year of hemp products under clinician guidance, and an FDA memo said it would not take action against qualifying oral CBD products furnished that way. A lawsuit against the pilot was dismissed for lack of standing and is on appeal.

what_changes.text: CBD products that stay under the cap, such as isolates without THC, can remain on shelves, but many full-spectrum products will exceed the 0.4 mg THC cap after 11 December 2026 unless reformulated.
Selling CBD in food, drinks or supplements remains outside FDA rules, and the new THC cap forces reformulation or relabeling of full-spectrum lines.
Some Medicare patients in participating ACO REACH and oncology models can receive hemp products through their providers; LEAD model participants follow from 1 January 2027.

timeline.event: 2018 Farm Bill removes hemp, including hemp-derived CBD, from the Controlled Substances Act
FDA says CBD needs a new regulatory pathway and denies supplement petitions

Federal judge dismisses challenge to the Medicare hemp pilot for lack of standing
D.C. Circuit sets briefing schedule in the appeal
Per-container THC cap applies to finished hemp products

faq.q: Is CBD legal in the US?
faq.a: Hemp-derived CBD is legal to produce and sell as a hemp product, but the FDA says it cannot be sold as a dietary supplement or added to food in interstate commerce. State rules vary.

faq.q: Will the hemp THC ban affect CBD?
faq.a: CBD itself stays hemp, but from 11 December 2026 any finished product with more than 0.4 mg of total THC and similar cannabinoids per container is excluded, which affects many full-spectrum products.
Not as a standard benefit. A CMS pilot lets participating providers in certain models furnish up to $500 a year of eligible hemp products; beneficiaries do not file Medicare claims for them.

faq.q: Is there an FDA-approved CBD drug?
faq.a: Yes, Epidiolex, approved for seizures linked to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex.
